doc.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021

title: Jazz audiences and a golden age of educated popular music
summary: Israels argues popular music was made and consumed by educated people from the late 19th century until the 1960s, when teen-market music displaced it.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I want to read something that came from your blog, and it has to do with that period of time I believe — I won’t read the whole thing but I found it quite interesting. “The musicians who grew up playing jazz in the U.S. in the 1940s and 50s had every reason to believe that they were pursuing their artistic activities in an atmosphere of common understanding with the members of the audience. Most musicians felt they were following or perhaps creating together a common aesthetic.” Why back then do you think the audience and the musicians were closer than I assume you think they are today?

It’s an essential question. And the answer to it is that I grew up in a most unusual period of time, one that I perceived from the inside as having been completely normal and it was in fact historically abnormal and that was a period in which, starting roughly in the late nineteenth century and going through to a little past the middle of the twentieth century, a period when popular music was created by and consumed by educated people. And that’s a most unusual historical phenomenon.
Well why has the increase — phenomenal increase in jazz education since the early 70s, can I extrapolate and say that you don’t think it has improved the audience for the music?

In small ways yes but mostly not. And it’s much bigger than the jazz education industry, and I use that word slightly pejoratively but not entirely. It just is a way to talk about it. The only other period that I know of in which popular art seemed also to be at this kind of high level is the period of Elizabethan theater. You know I’m talking about the period starting with Scott Joplin and Jelly Roll Morton and John Philip Sousa, that’s the late nineteenth century, and carrying through Louis Armstrong and the swing era and the bebop era, and all during that time jazz and popular music were connected. They were using the same material. There was a continuity of musical material and thought. It reached back, as a matter of fact it reached back hundreds of years back to Bach and beyond. And there was this musical continuity. You could see this developing over this, and this being added to this, and nothing more is really discarded, nothing was thrown away. In the mid-1960s when the baby boom generation reached adolescence that rich cultural era was decimated by this enormous population of teenagers who had money, not on purpose, it just was a socio-cultural event. So all these undeveloped people, and as we all were at thirteen, fourteen and fifteen, you and I and everyone else, all these

undeveloped people with money in their pockets became the target of the market machinery. And their music, their adolescent music and adolescent musical ideas, undeveloped musical ideas, took over and marginalized everything else. And that is, and now we’re in that system and have been there since roughly the mid-60s. It’s hard to put a date on it but, or the late 60s. And now I think we’re in a much more normal situation in which good cultural things are subsidized by institutions of educated and basically wealthy people. And that in general the popular music of the masses, the masses of all of these people whom I have every reason to love except about that, their music is now all disposable stuff and it won’t be — it has no durability at all — you will never remember a Beyoncé song or a Prince song. Those are not going to become cultural icons of America in spite of — no matter how many articles are written about them in The Atlantic or The New Yorker, they’ll be gone.
I don’t disagree with you but we probably could find people who do.
Oh we can find plenty of people who do. Absolutely. But they’re wrong.
